questions.q: What does loving your fate mean in Zen practice?
a: Accepting your life as it is instead of waiting for later
Resisting hardship to build stronger character
Changing your circumstances before choosing happiness
Postponing joy until your goals are met
questions.why: Lesson 1 says happiness comes from loving the life you already have.

questions.q: Why does the summary suggest turning problems into decisions?
a: You must choose anyway, so resistance only adds pressure
Decisions become easier when you avoid them
Problems disappear once you stop naming them
Other people should make big choices for you
questions.why: Lesson 2 says decision-making is simply the nature of life.

questions.q: What does impermanence represent in Zen, according to the summary?
a: A kind of perfection that makes room for renewal
A flaw to overcome through discipline
A reason to fear the future
A cycle only plants and animals follow
questions.why: Lesson 3 calls impermanence synonymous with perfection.

questions.q: Which philosophy does the summary compare Zen groundedness to?
a: Stoic acceptance of the present moment
Buddhist withdrawal from society
Western goal setting and ambition
Scientific rationalism and logic
questions.why: Lesson 1 notes Zen is similar to Stoic philosophy.

questions.q: How does the summary describe the role of death?
a: It clears space so that life can restart
It should be ignored while you are young
It makes every effort meaningless
It only matters to elderly people
questions.why: Lesson 3 says destruction allows life to recharge and restart.
